title: Spatiotemporal Graph Attention and Diffusion Forecasting on METR-LA
subtitle: with Simulated Adaptive Traffic Signal Control

authors.note: Team member names confirmed in canonical order.

abstract: We extend a frozen Phase 1 benchmark of local forecasters on METR-LA (207 loop detectors, 5-minute speeds) with graph models that also see neighbouring sensors: a Graph Attention Network (GAT) and a Diffusion Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network (DCRNN). All models share the Phase 1 chronological 70/10/20 split, 12-step history, horizons (5, 15, 30, 60 min) and valid-target mask. Hyperparameters are chosen on validation only; final models are trained with three seeds (one for the shuffled and DCRNN identity controls). To separate the road graph from model capacity we compare against a per-sensor GRU, an identity-graph ablation and a degree-preserving shuffled graph. Against the same architecture without neighbours (identity graph), GAT changes 60-minute test MAE by +0.189 [+0.154, +0.221] (positive = lower error, 95% paired day-block bootstrap interval); the pre-registered graph hypothesis H2 is contradicted because a degree-preserving shuffled graph also beat the identity graph (+0.040 [+0.026, +0.054] at 60 min), although the real graph beat the shuffled one (+0.149 [+0.124, +0.174]). H1 (GAT beats a per-sensor GRU at 30 and 60 min) is supported. DCRNN against its own identity-graph control changes 60-minute MAE by +0.650 [+0.507, +0.785]. Compared with the strongest Phase 1 model (XGBoost with historical-average features, 60-minute MAE 3.688), the best Phase 2 model (DCRNN) reaches 3.734; DCRNN has lower error at 15 and 30 min, and no detectable difference at 5 and 60 min (H0 contradicted). In a software simulation of one signalised approach driven by real test-period speeds and the models' real forecasts, the best Phase 2 forecast changed mean delay by +0.01 s per vehicle relative to the Phase 1 forecast, and even a perfect forecast only by +0.40 s; the large effect is adaptive versus fixed timing. All signal results are simulated.
blocks: Short-term speed forecasts feed ramp metering and signal timing. In Phase 1 of this capstone we built a local benchmark on METR-LA: persistence, historical average, Random Forest and XGBoost using only each sensor's own history. The best model, XGBoost with 36 features including historical-average profiles, reached a 60-minute test MAE of 3.688 source speed units, and error grew with horizon, consistent with models that cannot see conditions at neighbouring sensors.

Phase 2 asks one question, fixed before any result existed: does giving a forecaster neighbouring sensors through the road graph improve forecasts over equally capable models without the graph, on the same split, masks and history? We answer with pre-registered hypotheses whose verdicts are computed by code from paired bootstrap intervals. 'No detectable gain' was declared an acceptable answer. A separate, clearly simulated experiment feeds the forecasts into a signal-timing model.

DCRNN [1] combines bidirectional diffusion on the road graph with gated recurrent units. Graph Attention Networks [2] learn data-dependent weights over a node's neighbours. Tree ensembles [3], [4] are strong on engineered features but have no built-in way to use the graph. Kinematic-wave theory [8] motivates using neighbours, since congestion propagates along a corridor. Model-selection bias [7] motivates choosing hyperparameters on validation only and reporting controls tuned the same way.

Every deep model receives x of shape [12, 207, 7]: z-scored causally filled speed, a missing-reading flag, sine/cosine of time of day and day of week, and a weekend flag; it outputs z-scored speed for the four horizons. The loss is masked MAE in source speed units on valid targets only.

A shared temporal encoder (GRU or 1-D convolution) embeds each sensor's last hour (12 steps); multi-head masked attention mixes embeddings over graph neighbours (bidirectional road graph plus self-loops):
Logits of unconnected pairs are set to -10^9. Head outputs pass through a projection with a residual connection and a small head predicts the four horizons.
DCRNN applies K-hop forward and reverse random-walk diffusion on the directed graph inside a DCGRU encoder-decoder:
with P_f = D_out^-1 A and P_r = D_in^-1 A^T.

GRU Local is a shared per-sensor GRU with no spatial mixing. GAT identity and DCRNN identity are the same architectures on a self-loop-only graph, so any difference to the full model is the effect of the neighbours. GAT shuffled uses a node-permuted graph with the same degree structure (wrong neighbours). Controls reuse the hyperparameters tuned for their main model, which can slightly understate them.

The Phase 1 contract is reused through Phase 1's own loaders: chronological split (2012-03-01 to 2012-06-27, stored clock), unavailable readings (zero, negative, non-finite) excluded from loss and scoring, fill and scaling fitted on training data only. Origins are 23,967 / 3,416 / 6,844. Each deep family has four search candidates trained with seed 42 and scored on validation; the candidate with the lowest mean validation MAE is retrained with seeds 42, 43, 44 (one seed for the shuffled and DCRNN identity controls) and only these final runs predict the test period. Training uses Adam, batch 32-64, early stopping with patience 8 on validation MAE, and a wall-clock cap per run. The scorer reproduces every Phase 1 metric (maximum |MAE difference| 0.0e+00) and every Phase 1 bootstrap interval exactly.

Comparisons use Phase 1's paired circular moving-block bootstrap over stored days (2-day blocks, 2,000 resamples, seed 42); for multi-seed models each day's error sum is the mean over seeds. Peak/off-peak intervals use period-filtered day sums; contrasts between gains (H3, H4) are bootstrapped on the same resampled days. A comparison 'A beats B' is supported if the whole 95% interval of the MAE reduction is above zero, contradicted if below, inconclusive otherwise. Intervals are conditional on this test period and not adjusted for multiple comparisons.

A neighbour linked in both directions counts as both upstream and downstream, so those two shares can add up to more than the neighbour share. Attention shows what the model weighted, not how traffic propagates.

blocks: This is a software simulation, not traffic control. One signalised main approach (2 lanes) and a cross street (1 lane, 500 veh/h) are simulated cycle by cycle (90 s cycle, 10 s lost time, green 15-60 s) with Greenshields-shaped arrivals generated from speed and Webster uniform delay plus an overflow term [5]. Adaptive policies size green for the worst of the speed signals they see.

Experiment A (synthetic) uses synthetic speed profiles and synthetic forecasts with noise sized to measured test MAEs (local 2.97, graph 2.905 at 15 min). Experiment B uses real test-period weekday speeds (06:00-21:00) of the 30 sensors with the most proxy congestion (chosen from observed data only) and the models' actual test forecasts; every predictive policy sees the same signals and only the forecast source differs.

blocks: Code, run files, final configs, checkpoints and result tables are in the repository; 107 Phase 2 unit tests cover leakage, Phase 1 parity, graph handling, verdict logic and the simulator. Limits: (1) speeds are in source units (likely mph, unverified); (2) timestamps are on the stored clock (timezone unverified); (3) regions are coordinate boxes, not named freeways; (4) congestion is a proxy; (5) one chronological split of one city and season; (6) wall-clock caps and a 60-epoch limit bound training; all final runs used the same device (MPS, Table I), so runs that hit a cap reflect that device's speed; GAT stopped at the 60-epoch limit after 60 epochs; DCRNN stopped at the wall-clock cap after 14 epochs, so these models may be under-trained; (7) intervals are not adjusted for multiple comparisons; (8) attention weights are not evidence of traffic propagation; (9) signal results are simulated with an assumed demand rule.

We compared graph and non-graph forecasters under one leak-free protocol with code-computed verdicts. On this split, the road graph lowered GAT's error relative to the same model without neighbours (+0.189 [+0.154, +0.221] at 60 min), but a shuffled graph with the same degrees also helped (+0.040 [+0.026, +0.054]), so H2 as pre-registered is not supported: part of the gain comes from mixing information across sensors, not only from the true road links, while the real graph still beat the shuffled one (+0.149 [+0.124, +0.174]); GAT's 60-minute MAE is higher than the Phase 1 XGBoost + HA model, which uses features the deep models lack; DCRNN gained more from its graph (+0.650 [+0.507, +0.785] at 60 min against its identity control, one control seed); DCRNN, compared with XGBoost + HA, has lower error at 15 and 30 min, and no detectable difference at 5 and 60 min, without historical-average features, even though its training was cut by the wall-clock cap. In simulation, adaptive timing mattered far more than forecast accuracy.
